gloss: bend, bow down; palm of the hand, sole of the foot; hollow, pan; palm frond
summary: The verb is to bend or bow down: the head bowed like a rush, the soul bowed in distress, and those bowed down whom Yahweh raises erect (Isa 58:5; Psa 57:7; 145:14). כַּף is the hollow, curved flat of the hand, the palm, and of the foot, the sole; then the hand as what a man does and as the grasp of power, the palms spread in prayer or struck together, and other hollows: the sanctuary’s incense pans, the socket of the hip, the pocket of a sling. In Lev 23:40 the כַּפֹּת תְּמָרִים are palm fronds, as is כִּפָּה, the high frond set against the low rush (Isa 9:13). Akkadian kappu “hand, bowl” and kapāpu “bend”, Ugaritic kp and Arabic kaff “palm; scale pan”, and Aramaic כַּפָּא and כְּפַף show the same pairing of the curved hand with bending.

words.gloss: palm of the hand, hand; sole of the foot; hollow, pan, socket; palm frond
words.summary: The hollow of the hand, and then of the foot and of anything curved or cupped. Its 192 uses run from the literal palm that holds oil or flour, through the hand as a man’s deeds and as power over another, to fixed gestures (palms spread to God, palms struck in joy, scorn or pledge) and to vessels and hollows named from the cupped hand.

senses.definition: The inside of the hand, cupped to hold something, as distinct from the fingers; a palmful is a small measure.

evidence.note: The priest pours oil “on the palm of his own left hand” (עַל־כַּף הַכֹּהֵן הַשְּׂמָאלִית).
He dips “his right finger in the oil that is on his left כַּף”: the palm holds, the finger dips.
The widow has only “the fullness of a כַף of flour in the jar”: a palmful, the least of measures.
“Better a full כַף with quiet than two full fists (חָפְנַיִם) with toil.”
Aaron “filled his כַּף” from the grain offering and burned it.
Grass on the roof, with which the reaper does not fill his כַּף.
Samson scraped the honey out into his palms.
The parts of the ordination offering are put on the palms of Aaron and his sons and waved before Yahweh.
The grain offering of jealousy put on the woman’s palms.
The boiled shoulder put on the Nazirite’s palms.
“I put the cup into Pharaoh’s כַּף.”
“Though I weighed a thousand silver on my palms.”
The head of Dagon and “both the palms of his hands” cut off on the threshold.
Of Jezebel nothing was found but the skull, the feet and the palms of the hands.
“Behold, I have engraved you on my palms; your walls are continually before me.”
The early fig: “while it is still in his כַּף he swallows it.”
The princes “laid a כַף on their mouth”: silence.
A hand set Daniel trembling “on my knees and the palms of my hands”.

senses.gloss: hands, as what a man does
senses.definition: The palms as the doer of a man’s deeds: clean or guilty, toiling or slack, skilled or violent. Often beside the heart, the deed beside the will.

evidence.note: Who may ascend Yahweh’s hill: “the clean of palms (נְקִי כַפַּיִם) and pure of heart”.
Abimelech: “in the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my palms I have done this.”
“God has seen my affliction and the toil of my palms (יְגִיעַ כַּפַּי).”
“In vain I have cleansed my heart and washed my palms in innocence.”
“If I cleansed my palms with lye, yet you would plunge me in the ditch.”
“No violence in my palms, and my prayer is pure.”
David: “there is no wrong in my palms.”
“If there is iniquity in my palms.”
“Your palms are defiled with blood.”
“A deed of violence is in their palms.”
Nineveh is to turn “from the violence that is in their palms”.
“Both palms are on evil, to do it well.”
“The wicked is snared in the work of his own palms.”
“You shall eat the toil of your palms.”
The drought on “all the toil of palms”.
Job to God: “the toil of your palms”: himself, God’s work.
David led them “by the skill of his palms”.
“A slack palm makes poor, but the hand of the diligent makes rich.”
The capable wife works “with the delight of her palms”.
“Her palm she spreads to the afflicted, her hands she stretches to the needy.”
He who “shakes his palms from holding a bribe”.
“If any blot has stuck to my palms.”
Delivered “by the cleanness of your palms”.

senses.definition: The palm as what grips and holds: to be in someone’s כַּף is to be in his power, and to be delivered “from the כַּף” of an enemy is to be rescued from him. So too God’s palm laid on or over a man, and a man’s life (נֶפֶשׁ) taken in his own palm when he risks it.

evidence.note: “The king delivered us from the palm of our enemies and rescued us from the palm of the Philistines.”
Yahweh delivered David “from the hand (יַד) of all his enemies and from the כַּף of Saul”: the two words in parallel.
The surety “has come into the palm of your neighbour”: into his power.
“Yahweh has given us into the palm of Midian.”
The ark, “that it may save us from the palm of our enemies”.
Ahaz to Tiglath-pileser: save me from the palm of the king of Aram and the palm of the king of Israel.
“I will deliver you and this city from the palm of the king of Assyria.”
The remnant “escaped from the palm of the kings of Assyria”.
“I have given the beloved of my soul into the palm of her enemies.”
“I will redeem you from the palm of the terrible.”
“There Yahweh will redeem you from the palm of your enemies.”
To be delivered “from the palm of evil”.
“From the palm of the unjust and cruel.”
“He delivered us from the palm of the enemy and of him who lay in wait.”
“Are the palms of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand?”: are they already in your power?
“I will cover you with my palm until I have passed by”, and then “I will take away my palm” (Exo 33:23).
“You have hemmed me in behind and before, and laid your palm upon me.”
“Withdraw your palm far from me.”
God “covers the light with his palms”.
“Lay your palm on it”: on the beast no man can master.
Zion “a crown of beauty in the hand (יַד) of Yahweh and a royal turban in the palm of your God”.
“His palms were freed from the basket”: from Egypt’s burden.
Egypt the broken reed that pierces the palm of him who leans on it.
“You shall cut off her palm.”
Joab took three darts in his palm.
Elisha laid “his palms on his palms” over the dead child.
“On palms they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.”

senses.gloss: put one’s life in one’s palm: risk it
senses.definition: To set one’s נֶפֶשׁ, one’s life, in one’s own palm is to take it in hand where it may be lost: to risk death.

evidence.note: Jephthah: “I put my life in my palm and crossed over against the sons of Ammon.”
David “put his life in his palm and struck the Philistine”.
The woman of Endor: “I put my life in my palm and listened to your words.”
“Why do I take my flesh in my teeth and put my life in my palm?”
“My life is in my palm continually, yet I do not forget your law.”

senses.gloss: palms spread or lifted to God
senses.definition: The open palms spread out (פָּרַשׂ) or lifted up (נָשָׂא) toward God, toward the heavens or toward his house, as the posture of prayer; also spread out in anguish.

evidence.note: Solomon “spread out his palms toward the heavens” and prayed.
He had been “kneeling on his knees with his palms spread toward the heavens”.
“Let us lift up our heart with our palms to God in the heavens.”
“Let my prayer be set as incense before you, the lifting up of my palms as the evening offering.”
Moses: “I will spread out my palms to Yahweh”, and the thunder will cease.
Whoever “spreads out his palms toward this house”.
“I fell on my knees and spread out my palms to Yahweh my God.”
“In your name I will lift up my palms.”
“I have spread out my palms to you.”
“I will lift my palms to your commandments, which I love.”
“Lift up your palms to him for the life of your children.”
“If you prepare your heart and spread out your palms to him.”
“If we had spread out our palms to a strange god.”
“When you spread out your palms I will hide my eyes from you … your hands are full of blood.”
Daughter Zion “spreading her palms”, gasping, before her murderers.

senses.definition: The palm struck against the other palm or another’s: in acclaim and joy, in anger, scorn or grief over another’s fall, and as the handclasp that seals a pledge.

evidence.note: Joash crowned and anointed: “they struck palm (וַיַּכּוּ־כָף) and said, Let the king live!”
“All peoples, strike palm (תִּקְעוּ־כָף); shout to God with a voice of joy.”
“Let the rivers clap palm (יִמְחֲאוּ־כָף); let the mountains sing together.”
“All the trees of the field will clap palm.”
Balak’s anger burned and “he struck his palms together” (וַיִּסְפֹּק אֶת־כַּפָּיו).
All who pass by “clap their palms at you; they hiss and shake their head”: derision.
All who hear the news of Nineveh’s fall strike palm over it.
“Strike with your palm and stamp with your foot, and say, Alas!”
“Prophesy, and strike palm to palm”, with the sword doubled.
Yahweh: “I also will strike my palm to my palm, and I will satisfy my fury.”
“I have struck my palm at your dishonest gain and at your blood.”
“If you have become surety for your neighbour, have struck your palms for a stranger.”
“A man lacking heart strikes palm, becoming surety before his neighbour.”
“Do not be among those who strike palms, who are sureties for debts.”

senses.gloss: sole of the foot; paw, hoof
senses.definition: With רֶגֶל, the flat underside of the foot, where it treads and rests; of animals, the paw or hoof.

evidence.note: “Every place on which the sole of your foot treads shall be yours.”
The dove “found no rest for the sole of her foot”.
When “the soles of the feet of the priests” rest in the Jordan’s water, it will be cut off.
“Not so much as the treading of the sole of a foot.”
Among the nations “no rest for the sole of your foot”.
The delicate woman who would not set the sole of her foot on the ground.
Boils “from the sole of your foot to the crown of your head”: the whole body, bottom to top.
The adversary struck Job with boils from the sole of his foot to his crown.
Until Yahweh put his enemies under the soles of his feet.
“With the sole of my feet I have dried up all the streams of Egypt.”
Zion’s oppressors “will bow down at the soles of your feet”.
The wicked “ashes under the soles of your feet”.
“The place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, where I will dwell in the midst of the sons of Israel for ever.”
The living creatures: “the sole of their feet like the sole of a calf’s foot”: a hoof.
“Whatever goes on its palms, among all the animals that go on four”: paws, as against hoofs.

senses.gloss: hollow thing: pan, socket, pocket, handle
senses.definition: Things shaped like the cupped palm or holding as it holds: the small pans of the sanctuary that held incense, the hollow of the hip joint, the pocket of a sling, and the grips of a bolt.

evidence.note: Each prince’s gift: “one כַּף of ten gold, full of incense”: a small pan.
Twelve gold כַּפּוֹת full of incense, ten shekels each, a hundred and twenty in all.
Among the vessels of the table of the bread of the face, its כַּפֹּת.
Packed with the table for the march.
Solomon’s pans of gold.
Taken to Babylon with the rest of the bronze vessels.
He “touched the כַּף of his thigh, and the כַּף of Jacob’s thigh was dislocated”: the hollow socket of the hip.
The sinew “on the כַּף of the thigh” Israel does not eat.
The life of David’s enemies Yahweh will sling out “in the כַּף of the sling”: its pocket.
Myrrh dripped “on the כַּפּוֹת of the bolt”: its grips.

senses.definition: In כַּפֹּת תְּמָרִים, the fronds of date palms, taken with other branches at the feast of booths. Nehemiah, keeping the feast “as it is written”, calls the same thing עֲלֵי תְמָרִים, “leaves of palms”.

evidence.note: “You shall take for yourselves on the first day the fruit of goodly trees, כַּפֹּת תְּמָרִים, boughs of leafy trees and willows of the brook, and rejoice before Yahweh your God seven days.”
For the booths: olive, oil-tree, myrtle and עֲלֵי תְמָרִים, palm leaves, “as it is written”.

evidence.locator: Psa.91.12, כַּפַּיִם → χειρῶν; Psa.24.4 and Lam.3.41 the same; χείρ renders כַּף ×53

evidence.note: The adversary quotes Psa 91:12: “on χειρῶν they will bear you up”, the psalm’s כַּפַּיִם.
“Cleanse χεῖρας, you sinners, and purify hearts”: the clean palms and pure heart of Psa 24:4.
Men to pray “lifting up holy χεῖρας”: the palms lifted in prayer (Lam 3:41; Psa 141:2).

parallels.note: “Hand”, beside it in parallel and as the commoner word for the hand’s power.
“Heart”: clean palms and pure heart, the deed and the will.
“Fist, handful”: a palmful set against two fistfuls.

phrases.gloss: from the sole of the foot to the crown: the whole body
put one’s life in one’s palm: risk it
strike palm: clap in acclaim; clasp hands in pledge
strike the palms together (in anger or scorn)
the toil of the palms: what one labours for
from the palm of: out of the power of

words.summary: Five uses, all of bowing: the head bent like a rush, the soul bowed under distress, those bowed down whom Yahweh straightens, and a man bowing himself before God. The rarity is offset by Akkadian kapāpu and Aramaic כְּפַף, both “bend”, and by the Peshitta’s use of the root for bowing the knee.

stems.gloss: bend, bow down; (passive participle) bowed down

senses.definition: To bend down the head or the body; the passive participle is those bent low under trouble, the opposite of those Yahweh raises erect (זָקַף).

evidence.note: “Is it to bow down his head like a rush (לָכֹף כְּאַגְמֹן רֹאשׁוֹ) and spread sackcloth and ashes?”: the outward show of a fast.
“Yahweh upholds all who fall and raises up (זוֹקֵף) all the bowed down (הַכְּפוּפִים).”
“Yahweh opens the eyes of the blind; Yahweh raises up the bowed down; Yahweh loves the righteous.”
“They prepared a net for my steps; my soul is bowed down (כָּפַף נַפְשִׁי); they dug a pit before me.”

senses.definition: To bow oneself down in worship.

evidence.note: “With what shall I come before Yahweh, bow myself (אִכַּף) to the God on high? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings?”, answered in Mic 6:8.
“That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow (κάμψῃ)”; the Peshitta has this root here (תֵּכֻּוף).
“I bow (κάμπτω) my knees to the Father”; the Peshitta has this root.
“Every knee shall bow (κάμψει) to me”, quoting Isa 45:23 (Hebrew כָּרַע); the Peshitta has this root.

opposites.note: “Raise up erect”: what Yahweh does for the bowed down.

parallels.note: “The falling”, beside the bowed down whom Yahweh upholds.

words.summary: Three uses: twice the high palm frond set against the low rush as head against tail, once a tree’s branch that will not be green. It is the כַּף of Lev 23:40 in another form; whether the frond is named from the spread of the hand or from its bending (כָּפַף) the text does not say. No cognate of its own was found.

senses.definition: The frond at the top of a palm, standing for the high and honoured as the rush (אַגְמוֹן) stands for the low; and generally a tree’s branch.

evidence.note: “Yahweh will cut off from Israel head and tail, כִּפָּה and rush, in one day”; Isa 9:14 explains: the elder and honourable is the head, the prophet who teaches lies is the tail.
Of Egypt: no work that “head or tail, כִּפָּה or rush” can do: high and low alike.
The wicked: “his כִּפָּה will not be green”, a tree’s branch withering before its time.

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܟܦ (kap), for bowing the face or the knee, and in the passive participle ܟܦܝܦ, bent over. It shows the root’s bending sense in use in the apostles’ own time.

senses.gloss: bow (the face, the knee); bent over
senses.definition: To bow the face to the ground or the knee in worship; the passive participle, bent over and unable to stand straight.

evidence.note: A woman with a spirit of infirmity eighteen years, “bent over (ܟܦܝܦܐ) and unable to straighten herself at all”.
Jesus laid his hands on her, “and immediately she was made straight and glorified God”.
The women at the tomb, afraid, “bowed their faces to the ground”.
“Bow down their back always”, quoting Psa 69:24.
“Every knee shall bow to me”, quoting Isa 45:23.
“For this cause I bow my knees to the Father.”
“That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow.”

cognates.note: The same pairing as Hebrew כַּף: the hand and the small bowl shaped like it (Num 7:14).
The verb of the same root, beside kappu “hand”, as כָּפַף stands beside כַּף; Oracc also has kuppupu “very bent”.

cognates.gloss: palm (of the hand); tray, pan (of scales)
cognates.note: In KTU 1.24:35 kp mznm, the pans of the scales: the hollow-pan sense beside the palm.

evidence.locator: p. 113, *kpp: kp(m) ‘palm(s), hand(s), pan(s) of a scale’

cognates.gloss: hand, palm; a handful; paw of a beast; (kiffa) scale of a balance
cognates.note: Lane: “generally the hand: sometimes, apparently, the palm only”; “a handful; what one takes with the hand”; “often the paw of a beast”; and kiffa “a scale of a balance”. These answer to the palm, the palmful (1Ki 17:12), the paw (Lev 11:27) and the hollow pan. The Arabic verb kaffa of the same root is “refrain, restrain; hem a garment”, not “bend”.
Jewish Aramaic: palm and hand (Targ. Y. Gen 3:19; Targ. Psa 98:8, for the rivers’ clapping), and a pan or spoon, as the Hebrew’s hand and incense pan.
Jewish Aramaic, of bending trees into arches (Targ. II Esth 1:5) and in the Targum of Isa 58:5 for the bowing of the head; also “turn upside down”.

Attested once, for the sole of the foot in Ezk 1:7, so possibly taken from the Hebrew; Fisher argues the root is native from a Ge'ez *kafafa “be concave, bent”, the concave and the cupped hand being one idea. Recorded as possible until checked in a Ge'ez dictionary.
Punic, once: a curse on whoever “shall upset this stele” (CIS i 5510). It answers to the Aramaic “invert” of כְּפַף rather than to “bend”, so its tie to the Hebrew verb is possible only.

doctrine.statement: The palms stand for what a man does, set beside the heart, what he wills: the one who may ascend Yahweh’s hill is “clean of palms and pure of heart” (Psa 24:4), and Abimelech pleads “the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my palms” (Gen 20:5). Washing the palms cannot make a man clean before God (Job 9:30), and palms spread out in prayer while the hands are full of blood are not heard (Isa 1:15). James takes up the psalm’s pairing: “cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts” (Jas 4:8), and Paul asks for prayer “lifting up holy hands” (1Ti 2:8). From the verses: prayer is heard from those whose deeds and heart agree, and the cleansing scripture asks for is of both.

Jephthah, David, the woman of Endor and Job each speak of putting their נֶפֶשׁ, their soul, in their palm, and each means risking death: crossing to battle, facing Goliath, defying the king’s ban (Jdg 12:3; 1Sa 19:5; 1Sa 28:21; Job 13:14). The psalmist says “my soul is continually in my palm” (Psa 119:109) of a life in constant danger. In this idiom the soul is the life itself, held as something that can be lost, not a part of a man that survives his death.

Bowing the head “like a rush” with sackcloth and ashes is not the fast Yahweh chooses; he asks for bonds loosed and bread shared (Isa 58:5–7). When Micah asks whether to bow himself before the God on high with burnt offerings, the answer is “to do justice, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” (Mic 6:6–8). It is Yahweh who “raises up all the bowed down” (Psa 145:14; 146:8). Luke records a woman bent over for eighteen years, in the Peshitta ܟܦܝܦܐ, whom Jesus made straight with his hands (Luk 13:11–13): he did what the psalms say Yahweh does. From the verses: the bowing God accepts is of the life, not the posture, and the lifting up of the bowed down is his own work, shown in his Son.

note: Root key כפפ as the database keys it. BDB keys k.cn.ad and k.co.ab are cross-references (“see כפף”) with no tokens and are not claimed. כַּף is counted under k.cs.ab only. Lev 23:40 כַּפֹּת is the one use of כַּף for a frond; Neh 8:15’s עֲלֵי תְמָרִים is the parallel. The Jewish Aramaic כַּפָּא is also given the sense “top branch of a palm”, but only from a Talmudic discussion of Lev 23:40 itself, so it is not used as evidence for the frond. Not followed yet: a Ge'ez dictionary (Dillmann, Leslau) for kaf and *kafafa; Syriac ܟܦܬܐ “vault, hollow” and ܟܦܐ “palm, pan” in Payne Smith (not in SEDRA’s NT lexemes); the Syriac adjective ܟܦܝܦܐ (SEDRA lexeme 1565) has no NT tokens of its own in the database. The Arabic verb kaffa (“refrain; hem”, Lane p. 3001) does not share “bend” and is left in the ar-kaff note, not recorded as a cognate.
